chapter_theme: Four songs at Thiruvidaimarudur (திருவிடைமருதூர்): a whole life from a dewdrop of seed to the cremation fire, the miser who mocks the next world and dies despised, ending in a plea for union in which 'you and I' become one enjoyment; pleas for the gift of sweet Tamil, for the will to share and sing, and for the teaching of Siva-jnana against courtesans.
structure_note: 858 is a long biography of a worldly life; 859 and 861 are courtesan songs asking for song and for jnana teaching; 860 confesses the failure to sing and share.

858.reading: The poet traces a life: a drop small as dew on a grass tip becoming a body and a child whose prattle melts its parents, growing into a man with wives, house and halls, a miser who would not let a crumb of husk fall, who sends a poor ascetic asking for food to the upper house and the lower and leaps at him like a dog, follows a vain woman's word, serves vain men, mocks those who say there is a next world and scolds renunciants and brahmins; then poverty and diseases come, his eyes run, phlegm rises, his wife's mind changes and women and children say 'chee', he dreams of chariot and horse and the burning ground, his speech fails and breath leaves while kin wail and drums beat at the cremation ground among ghosts, and he is put into the fire. Against this he asks Murugan, destroyer of bonds, to grant the supreme bliss in which the two deeds, the three malas, death and birth end and 'you and I' become one enjoyment, at Idaimarudur, lord of the world and the gods.
858.nuance: The miser's sin is refusal, sending the begging ascetic from door to door (மேலை வீடு கேள் கீழை வீடு கேள்), and the denial of the next world (மறுமை உளதெனுமவரை ... வருவார்கள் போகுவார் காணுமோ எனா). The end is not escape to the feet but union: நீயும் நானுமாய் ஏக போகமாய், 'you and I as one enjoyment'. The line on what the devotees of the feet obtain (பெறுவதுவும் ஏசிடார்களோ) is hard to read.

859.reading: The poet describes women whose eyes reach their earrings as nets for young men's lives, whose lips he drinks and whose breasts he embraces in growing passion, and asks whether Murugan will not grant him the grace to sing sweet poems in order, with knowledge of release ripening, in rare Tamil sound, joined to a worship of bright speech. The praise tells how the vel shattered Meru and the sea, how Murugan rode the peacock to restore the gods and destroy cruel deeds, spoke silent teaching into the ear of his father who dances with ghosts, married the hunter girl, and as Kumara guru sought debate so that the Jains played on the stakes, lord of the great sages of Idaimarudur.
859.nuance: தாதை செவி நிறைய மவுன உரையாடு: Murugan fills his father's ear with a 'silent' teaching, the Om story without naming Om. அமணர் கழுவில் விளையாட வாது படை கருது குமரகுருநாத: the impaling of the Jains, the Sambandar story, given to Murugan as Kumaraguru.

860.reading: The poet confesses that he never once went to sing calmly 'Kumara, six-faced one of sweet red speech, the first who came in Saravana, Kandha', the one whom Sankara himself worships, Sankara whom Vishnu, Brahma, the Vedas and the gods cannot praise and who wears serpents, Ganga, moon, konrai and thumbai in his hair; that he never came near with the grace to share even a millet grain; and asks whether he will not think of the vow of walking in the way of tapas. The praise shows the vel splitting the demons skilled in mantra and tantra while vultures, foxes and ghosts feast and dance, names Murugan the great guru of Idaimarudur, lover of the forest maiden, whose lotus feet with ruby anklets, raining compassion, the gods stroke in service as their final refuge.
860.nuance: The confession is of three omissions: not singing, not sharing (பகிர ஒரு தினையளவு), not keeping to tapas, so the remedy is the same as in 23, sharing even a millet grain. சங்கரன் கும்பிடும் குமரன்: Siva worships Murugan. The opening list of who cannot praise Siva is long and its division tentative.

861.reading: The poet speaks of the women who sell themselves in public with civet- and rose-water-scented breasts and arrow eyes, says that he, a dog who does not melt like wax, suffers confusion, delusion and anguish and is entangled in mala and maya, and asks Murugan to come and give his bountiful teaching of Siva-jnana. The praise shows the seven hills fleeing, the sea roaring, the demon army broken and the gods freed while dogs, jackals and vultures feast, names the hero on the elephant and the young peacock, 'victory, Muruga, Guha, Kandavel', and the lord of Idaimarudur where the Kaveri beats its banks.
861.nuance: பொதுவினில் விலைகூறு மாதர்: women who name their price in public. மெழுகென உருகாவனார் turns the usual image round: he does not melt like wax for the Lord. சிவஞான போதகம், the teaching asked for, is also the name of Meykandar's Saiva Siddhanta text; whether the poet means the book is uncertain.

links.note: Both begin the body as a drop like dew on a blade of grass; the Tirumanthiram follows the drop through the body's elements, 858 follows it through a whole life to the cremation fire.
Both trace life from a dewlike drop to death; 508 ends asking whether the sorrow will never end, 858 asks for a union in which 'you and I' become one.
Both name as remedy the sharing of even a millet grain (தினையளவு); in 23 it is drawn from the fear of death, in 860 it stands with singing and tapas among the poet's omissions.

859 credits Kumaraguru with the debate in which the Jains played on the stakes (அமணர் கழுவில் விளையாட வாது படை கருது குமரகுருநாத). 865 praises Murugan for taking those who imprisoned the loving ascetics of the Lord and setting them on the stake, while vultures pecked (கழு நெஞ்சிலே ஏற). Both give Murugan the impaling of the enemies of Saiva devotees, the Sambandar story in 859 named as Jains, in 865 as asuras.

860 confesses three omissions: he never went to sing the Lord's praise calmly, never shared even a millet grain's worth (பகிர ஒரு தினையளவு பண்புகொண்டு அண்டிலன), and never thought of the vow of walking in tapas. Tirumanthiram 264 rebukes those who do not praise the Supreme (பரமனை ஏத்தார), do not give even a little to beggars (ஈதலை யாயினும் ஈயார்), and do not tend groves, and asks if they will stand in hell. The song makes the Tirumanthiram's charge a first-person confession, with praise and the smallest gift heading both lists.

861 calls the poet one who does not melt like wax (மெழுகென உருகாவனார்), tangled in mala and maya, and asks the Lord to come and give Siva-jnana teaching. Tirumanthiram 272 says that no fierce penance reaches the gem, only those who melt with love and soften within (அன்போடு உருகி அகங்குழைவார்க்கு அன்றி). Both make melting the condition; the song counts its absence among the poet's faults and asks grace to supply what he cannot.

source_issues: Song 858: உ றவின்முறை and உ மிழுமது (lines 18, 22) are split by a space after உ.
